title: Advice/relationship-support register
description: This latent fires on the characteristic language of advice-column or interpersonal-support text: short conversational openers and closers ('Hey!', 'Thanks for chatting with me.', 'Would you like some help with that?'), empathetic perspective-taking phrases ('However, it's essential to consider X's feelings/perspective as well'), and hedged suggestions about what 'might have' helped or avoided a problem ('This might help alleviate any concerns', 'This could have avoided the issue'). It activates broadly across advice/AITA/relationship-coaching style text on conversational scaffolding, empathy statements, and speculative causal/counterfactual remarks about interpersonal situations, regardless of the specific topic (finances, relationships, health, career). It does not activate on purely factual, technical, or narrative content lacking this advisory/conversational-empathy framing, such as plain descriptive statements or list items that don't involve interpersonal reasoning or hedged suggestion-giving.

title: Empathetic advice-column reassurance
description: This latent fires on the discourse patterns typical of relationship/advice-column responses: reassuring or validating phrases that soften judgment ('it's not about being the bad guy', 'you're not alone', 'it's understandable that...'), transitional or list-scaffolding markers that introduce suggestions or steps ('Here are some tips to consider:', 'Instead of...', numbered/bulded list starters), and framing statements that set up a reflective or advisory stance (e.g., 'In hindsight, it might have been better...', 'Considering the circumstances...'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic transition/framing fragments (like 'Instead of', 'approx.', bullet markers, bolded headers) that structure advice-giving text, and on reassurance/validation clauses embedded in interpersonal advice narratives. It would NOT activate on plain factual or narrative statements unrelated to advice-giving or emotional validation (e.g., biographical facts, technical descriptions) that lack this scaffolding or empathetic-reassurance framing, even if they discuss similar interpersonal topics.

title: Validating the user's feelings and innocence
description: This latent fires on advice-column style statements that reassure the addressee ('you') that their feelings, reactions, or decisions are valid and that they are not at fault ('You're not the asshole', 'You're not being unreasonable', 'You're right to feel...'). It activates on second-person absolution or validation clauses that explicitly negate blame, wrongness, or unreasonableness, or that affirm a right/entitlement to a feeling or action, typically in relationship-advice or interpersonal-conflict contexts. It also extends to closely related moves like empathetic acknowledgment of the other party's possible feelings ('It's understandable that...', 'Maybe they felt...') when framed to excuse the user's behavior. It does NOT activate on purely descriptive or narrative sentences that recount events without a normative judgment about fault or feelings (e.g., factual background details, plain requests, or neutral suggestions lacking any validating/absolving framing).

title: Personal-advice-column supportive guidance
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/self-help style discourse offering supportive, empathetic guidance to a person about their emotions, relationships, or personal choices—e.g., suggestions to pursue joyful activities, set boundaries, reflect on feelings, communicate openly, or 'treat yourself.' It activates on generic reassurance phrases ('we've all been there'), validating statements ('it's understandable that...'), and formulaic advice-giving constructions (imperative + rationale, e.g. 'Make time for activities that bring you joy'), typically addressed directly to 'you' in a warm, coaching tone. It does not activate on neutral factual, technical, or procedural statements lacking this empathetic/advisory framing (e.g., instructions for registering a trademark, pressing tofu, or describing sirens as warning signals), even though some such sentences appear in the list due to co-occurring latents—the key trigger is the emotionally supportive, advice-column register rather than the topic itself.

title: Advice-list items in interpersonal guidance
description: This latent fires on short, imperative or bullet-style clauses that appear as discrete steps or recommendations in advice-giving text, typically about relationships, communication, or personal conduct (e.g., 'Discuss your concerns...', 'Try to let go of...', 'Ask open-ended questions'). It also activates on the numbered/bulleted list scaffolding itself (bare markers like '2.', '3. **', '5.') that structures such advice, and on short imperative or reflective fragments that cap off a piece of relationship/self-help guidance. It is largely agnostic to the specific topic (dating, workplace boundaries, jaw pain, finances) and instead responds to the structural/functional role of being a discrete recommended action or list item within advice-style prose. It does not activate strongly on long explanatory or narrative sentences that lack this imperative/list-item, advice-step quality, such as factual statements, extended justifications, or descriptive background context.

title: Actionable self-improvement advice items
description: This latent fires on imperative, list-formatted advice items (often bolded headers like 'Attend school events**:' or 'Practice mindfulness**:') that prescribe concrete lifestyle, productivity, or self-care actions—e.g., attending events, building routines, networking, setting goals, celebrating milestones. It activates most strongly on terse, bullet-like recommendations for building habits, social connections, or personal/professional development, typically framed as generic 'how-to improve your life' tips rather than advice tied to a specific relational conflict. It activates less on sentences addressing interpersonal emotional dynamics, communication in specific relationships, or reflective/empathetic statements about someone else's feelings (e.g., 'listen to your friend', 'communicate openly with your mom'), which instead trigger a related but distinct relationship-advice latent.

title: 'This can/will help' benefit-explanation clause
description: This latent fires on the templated construction '[This/These] + can/will/helps to + [verb], often followed by a list of positive psychological or relational outcomes (feel more confident, connected, motivated, relaxed, etc.). It activates most strongly on short, self-contained sentences whose main syntactic job is to state that some action or habit produces a beneficial effect, typically in generic self-help or advice-giving prose. It is largely agnostic to the specific topic (relationships, productivity, parenting, stress) and instead tracks the grammatical/rhetorical pattern of asserting a causal benefit using 'help(s)' as the pivot verb. It does not activate on sentences that describe a benefit without this 'help' framing, that make negative or cautionary claims (e.g. 'This can lead to defensiveness'), or that are full advice statements/imperatives without the help-clause structure, though such sentences may still activate related latents due to similar topical content.

title: Reassuring self-care advice closer
description: This latent fires on concluding, empathetic advice sentences that reassure the reader and urge self-compassion or self-prioritization, typically in the context of emotional/relationship advice (e.g., 'Remember, taking care of yourself is essential', 'Be kind to yourself', 'You're not alone'). It activates most strongly on short, formulaic imperative or reminder phrases—often beginning with 'Remember,' 'Be patient/kind,' or 'Take care of yourself'—that validate the reader's feelings, normalize imperfection, and stress well-being, boundaries, or self-worth as a wrap-up statement. It does not activate on purely factual, descriptive, or narrative sentences, nor on advice that focuses on the other person's needs, practical logistics, or analytical reasoning without this comforting/self-affirming framing; sentences must carry that soothing, reassuring 'take care of yourself/you're doing fine' tone rather than just discussing relationships or emotions generally.

title: Empathetic advice-column validation
description: This latent fires on the characteristic language of advice-giving/counseling responses, especially validating phrases that acknowledge a person's feelings or situation ('it's understandable that...', 'it sounds like...', 'that's okay') before offering guidance, as well as related actionable advice steps, communication tips, and reflective questions typical of relationship/personal-advice text (e.g., 'try using I statements', 'ask her what's bothering her', practical checklist items like test-driving a car or setting up transfers). It activates on sentences with an empathetic, second-person advisory tone addressing someone's emotional or practical dilemma, including validation statements, suggested actions, and clarifying questions posed to the advice-seeker. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, narrative descriptions without advisory framing, or third-person analytical text that doesn't address 'you' in a supportive/coaching register (e.g., pure data, definitions, or unrelated technical content).

title: Framing a tricky situation as a 'conundrum'/dilemma
description: This latent fires on phrases that explicitly frame a described situation as a puzzling dilemma or tricky scenario, most often the word 'conundrum' (frequently preceded by 'The eternal/classic/age-old conundrum!') but also related framing like 'scenario!', 'dilemma', or transitional set-up phrases that introduce advice-giving ('Some suggestions for moving forward:', 'Let's tackle this together', 'Here's a breakdown of...'). It activates strongly on short, often exclamatory labeling statements that name or announce a relational/social predicament before elaborating on it, and on empathetic advice-column openers that acknowledge a hard situation. It does NOT activate on plain descriptive or advice content itself (e.g., specific tips, factual claims, or validating statements like 'you're not the asshole') unless paired with this dilemma-framing language, nor on neutral narrative sentences that don't cast something as a puzzle or introduce a structured solution list.

title: Validating/advice-giving assistant tone in interpersonal advice
description: This latent fires on the characteristic register of an AI assistant (or advice-giver) responding to a personal/relationship dilemma: validating the user's feelings or actions ('You're not being selfish...', 'It's great that you're aware...'), gently judging a third party's behavior ('They should have respected that'), offering supportive reassurance ('Don't let fear stop you', 'They don't define your worth'), or issuing brief advice-column-style directives and stock openers ('I'm happy to help you with that!', 'Honesty is usually the best policy'). It activates on short, declarative, emotionally-supportive or normative statements embedded in advice/therapy-style text (e.g., Reddit relationship-advice responses), including validation of effort/time invested, calls to set boundaries, and rhetorical soothing phrases. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, technical instructions without an interpersonal/emotional framing, or narrative description that lacks this evaluative, advice-giving, second-person validating stance.

title: Advice-list formatting and structure markers
description: This latent fires on the structural scaffolding of advice-giving text produced by an assistant persona: numbered/bulleted list markers (e.g., '1.', '2. **', '3.'), bolded item headers that introduce a tip or category ('Ask for advice**:', 'Investing:**', 'Pros and Cons:**'), and short framing/transition phrases that organize conversational self-help content ('One step at a time', 'Take things one step at a time', section headers like '**Alternatives:**' or '**Reflections and insights:**'). It activates most strongly on bare or near-bare list-numbering tokens and bolded sub-headers within advice enumerations, and more weakly on related conversational filler (exclamatory asides, rhetorical questions, empathetic acknowledgments) that co-occurs in the same advice-column style text. It would not activate on plain narrative or factual prose lacking list/enumeration structure or on advice content that is not formatted as a numbered/bulleted, bolded breakdown, even if the topic (relationships, self-improvement, etc.) is similar.

title: Reassuring, validating advice-column commentary
description: This latent fires on the characteristic register of advice/support responses (e.g., Reddit AITA or relationship-advice style text): short reassurances ('and that's okay!', 'that's something to be celebrated'), validation of the reader's feelings or actions ('you're not the asshole', 'that's a valid point'), normalizing statements ('it's natural to feel...'), and gentle framing of a neutral, understanding advisor stance ('I'm here to offer a neutral perspective', 'let's weigh the pros and cons'). It activates on sentences that soothe, validate, excuse, or reframe someone's behavior/emotions as understandable or okay, often using stock reassurance phrases and second-person address. It does not activate on purely factual, instructional, or neutral descriptive sentences that lack this validating/reassuring emotional stance (e.g., recipe steps, job descriptions, or plain questions asking for information), even if they occur in similar advice-style text.

title: Empathetic validation in relationship advice
description: This latent fires on advice-giving language that validates or normalizes the reader's feelings, situation, or dilemma, typically in the context of interpersonal, relationship, or emotional-support advice (e.g., 'It's understandable that you're feeling...', 'I understand that...', 'That's completely normal'). It activates strongly on empathetic framing phrases that acknowledge emotions before offering guidance, as well as related advice-column boilerplate like suggesting communication, setting boundaries, or reassurance that something 'isn't a reflection of your worth.' It also picks up on generic advice-list scaffolding (numbered/bolded list markers, 'Establish boundaries', 'Host events') that commonly accompanies this therapeutic advice register. It does NOT activate on neutral factual statements, narrative description, or advice-adjacent content lacking any validating/empathetic or supportive framing, such as plain instructions, statistics, or unrelated declarative facts.

title: First-person relational scripting ('I' statements)
description: This latent fires on first-person, direct-address sentences that model interpersonal communication scripts—typically quoted or suggested things one person could say to another to express feelings, set boundaries, apologize, check in, or negotiate a relationship issue. It activates strongly on template phrases like 'I just wanted to,' 'I know you...,' 'I feel like,' 'Can we talk/talk about,' and 'I'll make sure to,' especially when embedded in advice-giving contexts (e.g., 'You could say something like...') that model empathetic or assertive dialogue. It is largely indifferent to topic (dogs, holidays, relationships, work) but keyed to the interpersonal, first/second-person conversational register rather than third-person description or analysis. It does NOT activate on purely descriptive, third-person narrative sentences that recount events or judge behavior without being framed as something someone says or could say directly to another person (e.g., 'She didn't even have the decency to tell you...' as narration, or evaluative statements like 'It's not fair to ask someone to spend their own money'), since those lack the direct first-person scripted-speech quality.

title: Advice-column relational guidance
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/therapy-style text that offers interpersonal guidance, validation, or practical suggestions—phrases that acknowledge feelings, suggest reflective questions ('What are my true feelings for this person?'), recommend concrete steps ('Consider keeping it in a charger...', 'Join online communities...'), or use empathetic hedging language ('I understand that...', 'It's possible that...', 'What works for one person may not work for another'). It activates on the conversational, second-person or first-person advice register common in relationship, self-help, or conflict-resolution writing, including stock reassurances ('the benefits outweigh the drawbacks'), suggested scripts for difficult conversations, and lists of self-improvement tips. It does NOT activate on purely factual, technical, or narrative statements lacking this advisory/empathetic framing—e.g. plain descriptions of events, statistics, or neutral information without a guiding or validating tone toward a person's feelings or choices.

title: Interpersonal advice-column reasoning
description: This latent fires on sentences from advice/therapy-style text that analyzes interpersonal conflicts and coaches assertive, boundary-setting communication: validating the person's feelings, reframing others' behavior, asserting rights ('you're not obligated to...'), and offering scripts or techniques for expressing needs respectfully. It activates on evaluative statements about someone's rudeness/insensitivity, advice to communicate assertively or calmly, permission-granting statements about autonomy and boundaries, and suggested reframes of negative thoughts into constructive ones. It does not activate on neutral factual, narrative, or procedural content unrelated to relationship dynamics or emotional communication (e.g., safety statistics, business plans, technical instructions), even if phrased as advice, since the core trigger is guidance around interpersonal emotional/assertiveness dynamics rather than advice-giving in general.

title: Advice-column empathetic framing
description: This latent fires on the stock rhetorical scaffolding of advice/Reddit-style responses: exclamatory framing phrases ('Congratulations!', 'Wow, what a wild ride!', 'The complex web of relationships!'), validating or reassuring openers ('It's understandable that...', 'Firstly, congratulations on...'), acronym shorthand from advice forums (WIBTA, NTA), and light empathetic transitional statements that acknowledge feelings before giving advice. It activates on short, formulaic, emotionally-toned phrases that structure or soften interpersonal advice-giving, rather than on the substantive content or factual claims themselves. It would not activate on neutral factual statements, technical explanations, or advice content that lacks this validating/exclamatory rhetorical wrapper (e.g., plain instructions like 'apply for the program through their website' without an empathetic frame).

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral tokens that begin items in an enumerated list (e.g., '2.', '3.', '4.'), often followed by markdown bold formatting. It activates on the digit-plus-period token itself, regardless of the list's topic, appearing consistently in sequences of instructions, steps, tips, or reasons. It does not activate on the surrounding prose content of the list items, on bullet points using dashes or asterisks alone, or on numbers used in non-list contexts like dates, quantities, or citations.

title: Empathetic advice-column validation and reframing
description: This latent fires on the characteristic voice of an advice-giver (e.g., relationship/personal-advice chatbot) that validates the user's feelings or situation, reframes their behavior in understanding terms, or gently restates/summarizes what the user did or is feeling before offering guidance. It activates on phrases like 'You're doing the best you can,' 'It sounds like you're...,' 'It's understandable that...,' 'Firstly, kudos to you for...,' and similar empathetic, second-person framings that acknowledge emotions, motives, or circumstances. It does not activate on neutral factual statements, instructions/lists without empathetic framing, or third-person narrative content unrelated to validating someone's feelings or actions (e.g., factual trivia, martial arts descriptions, travel destination facts), even if those appear in similar advice-style text.
